abstract: Agricultural intensification has led to a decline of farmland bird populations worldwide. Most studies have focused on the role of practices on birds during the breeding season but little is known about the role of practices during winter. Here, we study the effect of different types of winter field cover and landscape features on wintering birds in the rice production area of the Camargue (Rhone delta, France). We conducted bird surveys in 86 organic crop fields during winter. We hypothesized that the type of field cover (rice stubble, bare ground, winter wheat, grasslands), and the type of landscape features (hedegrows, grass strips and reed strips) have an effect on the abundance and species richness of wintering bird communities at field level. Moreover, we hypothesized that the diversity of field cover types and landscape features at the landscape level have a positive effect on the abundance and species richness of wintering bird communities, in line with the landscape complementation hypothesis. Results show that at the field level, rice stubble fields accommodate higher bird abundance that fields with other cover types. Moreover, we show that this pattern is driven by a few gregarious and granivorous wintering species while others preferred grasslands. At the landscape level, we show that the diversity of landscape features increased wintering bird abundance. We also show species-specific responses to different types of landscape features with hedgerows, reed strips and grass strips affecting diverse species at both field and landscape levels. Overall, our results suggest that rice stubble provide important winter habitats for declining granivorous species, while maintaining a heterogeneous mosaic of landscape features benefits wintering bird communities. Finally, we quantify species-specific response to the surface of different landscape features, a key step to build-up dedicated agri-environmental schemes.
